### Purpose Statement

This guidance provides safe patching and update strategies for multi-tenant cloud environments (AWS & Azure), focusing on zero-downtime approaches to maintain service availability while ensuring security compliance.

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#background]

### Background

In multi-tenant cloud environments (where **shared infrastructure** serves multiple accounts or subscriptions), applying patches and updates with **minimal downtime** is critical. Even brief outages can impact numerous customers at once, leading to revenue loss, SLA penalties, and damage to trust.

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#background-details]

## Background Details

In multi-tenant cloud environments (where **shared infrastructure** serves multiple accounts or subscriptions), applying patches and updates with **minimal downtime** is critical. Even brief outages can impact numerous customers at once, leading to revenue loss, SLA penalties, and damage to trust. Modern DevOps practices and cloud platforms emphasize **zero-downtime deployments** -- treating planned outages as an outdated practice for SaaS.
page_texts.7:
[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#problem]

## Problem

Gainwell IT Operations struggles with patching issues in the wake of multiple tenants limiting windows of opportunity to conduct patching using traditional means, which require downtime. Often, the patch window has come and gone before testing of the patch's success can be performed, leading to failures which were not detected during the original patch window.

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#objective]

## Objective

Perhaps a new approach to patching, especially in multi-tenant cloud environments, should be considered. This paper presents a comprehensive review of frameworks and tools for safe, efficient patching in AWS and Azure, followed by a recommended approach to achieve resilient updates. The targeted outcomes of a safe and efficient patching approach is to
minimize or avoid planned downtime will reducing or eliminating error.

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#key-frameworks-for-zero-downtime-updates]

## Key Frameworks for Zero-Downtime Updates

To update cloud services without disrupting users, the industry relies on several proven deployment strategies. These frameworks handle updates in ways that limit the blast radius of any issues and keep the service running:

| **Strategy** | **How It Works (Summary)** | **Reliability & Risk Mgmt.** | **Downtime Mitigation** | **Rollback Capabilities** | **Use in Multi-Tenant Environments** |
|--------------|----------------------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| **Blue-Green Deployment** *(maintain two environments -- one "blue" (live) and one "green" (staging with new updates); switch traffic to green after testing)* | Two parallel production environments are maintained. The new version (green) is deployed separately while the old (blue) continues serving users [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Once the green environment passes tests, user traffic is switched over (e.g., via load balancer or DNS change) to make it live [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). | New release is fully vetted in an identical environment before exposure [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). This isolates any issues to the green environment during testing. If a bug appears, it affects only the new environment (no real users yet). | Near-zero downtime: switching user traffic to green is virtually instantaneous (a load balancer flip). Users see no outage during the cutover because the old version was running until the moment of switch [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Any needed data migrations can be done beforehand in background. | Instant rollback: If problems occur after going live, switch traffic back to the blue environment immediately [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Since blue hasn't changed, it's a safe fallback. Rollback is as quick as the original switch (just repoint the router or DNS). | Common in SaaS updates. All tenants can be moved to the new version in one go, or tenant-by-tenant cutovers can be done by onboarding a few tenants to green first as a pilot [[2]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates). A challenge is database changes -- shared databases must be compatible with both versions during transition, or use a dual-write/replication strategy [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). |
| **Canary Release** *(gradually roll out the new version to a subset of servers or users/tenants, observe, then expand)* | The update is initially deployed to a small portion of the environment (or a small subset of users) -- the "canary" group [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). For example, 5% of application instances (or specific canary tenants) run the new code while the rest run the old code. System behavior is closely monitored. If all looks good, progressively increase the rollout to more servers or users. | Limits risk by exposing only a small fraction of real traffic to the new update initially [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Any severe bug will impact only the canary users, not everyone. This early feedback loop greatly reduces the chance of a widespread failure. | No global downtime: Most users remain on the old stable version initially. The service as a whole remains up. Even canary users typically experience the service, just potentially with new features or minor hiccups if the update isn't perfect. The rollout can be halted at any time, ensuring any issue is contained. | Quick halt or rollback: If errors are detected in the canary, the deployment can be stopped. The canary instances can be removed from rotation or reverted to the old version quickly. Since the new version wasn't fully deployed, pulling it back is straightforward (e.g., redirect canary users to stable servers) [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Many CI/CD systems can automate this: they halt further rollout and trigger rollback on any health check failure. | Widely used for multi-tenant SaaS: Typically implemented with deployment "rings" or stages [[2]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates). For example, internal users or a small customer segment get the update first, then a bigger set, then all tenants. Tenants might be tagged as *early adopters* vs *general release*. This way, you protect the majority while testing on a representative subset. It requires the ability to route specific tenants to specific app instances (feature flags or routing rules often help achieve this). |
| **Rolling Update** *(update servers or containers in batches, one after the other, until all are updated)* | Instead of updating everything at once, updates are applied to one server/group at a time while others continue serving traffic. For example, update 1 out of 10 instances, wait for it to pass health checks, then update the next, and so on [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). In container platforms, this is often orchestrated automatically. | Changes are introduced gradually, limiting the impact of any single update to a fraction of servers. If something goes wrong on one instance, it's detected before affecting all. The service capacity is slightly reduced during updates, but not completely taken down. Health checks ensure each instance is stable before proceeding [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). | No total downtime: because other instances carry the load while one is being updated [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Users might not notice anything aside from perhaps a slight capacity reduction (which is mitigated by slight over-provisioning or auto-scaling). Rolling updates can achieve zero downtime if the system is designed to handle N-1 capacity. | Stop-and-fix rollback: If the update fails on a particular instance, the rolling process can pause. In orchestration systems (Kubernetes, Service Fabric), if a new instance fails a health check, the rollout will stop and optionally start replacing the failed update with a previous version [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). Manual intervention can trigger rollback on already updated ones (essentially treating it like a partial canary failure). Rollback isn't as instant as blue-green, but you typically only have to fix a subset rather than the whole fleet. | Standard for large fleets (e.g., OS patching on thousands of VMs). All tenants remain served, as some instances are always running the old version until the end. However, during the process, different tenants may be on different versions. Backwards compatibility is crucial -- the new code must work with data or inputs from tenants still on the old code [[4]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/devops/operate/achieving-no-downtime-versioned-service-updates). In practice, this means avoiding breaking changes or supporting both versions until the rollout finishes. |
| **Immutable Image Deployments** *("replace instead of modify": deploy new VMs/containers with updates baked in, rather than patching in-place)* | Rather than applying changes to running servers, you build a new machine image or container image that has the update (a patched OS or new app code) and deploy new instances from this image [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). The old instances are then terminated or phased out. For example, use a new AMI for EC2 Auto Scaling, or a new container tag for Kubernetes, and let the orchestrator launch new pods while killing old ones. | Ensures each updated instance starts from a clean, tested state (the new image is tested in advance). This avoids "configuration drift" issues or patch failures on certain long-lived servers -- every server is fresh and identical. AWS calls this *preferred* because you always deploy in a known good state [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). The risk of leftover issues from previous versions is eliminated. | Usually accomplished via a blue-green or rolling deployment of the new instances, so downtime can be zero (new instances come up behind the scenes, only cutting over when ready) [[5]][https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html]([3)](<https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/>). If using a rolling approach, it's essentially a rolling update but each instance is replaced by a clean one. If using blue-green with images, you launch a parallel green stack from the new image. Either way, existing running version handles traffic until new ones are proven. | Simple rollback by image revert: Keep the previous version's image handy -- if the new image has problems, you can redeploy using the last image (or simply continue running the old instances if you used blue-green). In AWS, for example, you might just undo the Auto Scaling update to use the old AMI. Because no in-place changes were made to the old instances, they're still available unchanged if needed [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). | Considered best practice for cloud ops. Multi-tenant SaaS providers often use this to patch OS or base environments: e.g., build a "golden image" each month with the latest patches [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html), then roll it out. Also, a "deployment stamp" model is used where each set of tenants runs on a stamp (a full stack); new stamps (with new images) can be deployed one by one [[3]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). This limits blast radius -- e.g., update one stamp while others still run the old version for other tenants. |
| **Feature Flags** *("dark launch" new code paths, toggle features on or off at runtime)* | Deploy new code that includes new features or changes *turned off by default*. A configuration flag in the app determines whether the new code path runs [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). After deployment, you can turn the feature on for all or a subset of users instantly by flipping the flag (no redeploy needed). If something goes wrong, flip it off. This allows separating code deployment from feature exposure. | Greatly reduces risk of bad deployments: The new code is deployed but dormant. You can test it live with a small set of users by enabling the flag just for them. If the code has a bug, it's switched off before most users ever see it [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). This avoids the "all-or-nothing" release problem by making releases incremental and easily reversible. | No service restart needed: Toggling a feature flag doesn't require shutting down servers -- it's an in-memory setting or config change. So you can effectively deploy a new feature without *any* downtime. If a feature is causing errors, turning it off immediately stops the errors, without rolling back the entire deployment [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). This keeps the app running continuously. | Instant rollback of functionality: If a new feature misbehaves, you *immediately* disable it via the flag (often through a management console). This is faster than a traditional rollback which might involve redeploying old code. The problematic code remains deployed but inert, which is acceptable as a short-term mitigation [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). Full rollback may not be needed if the flag-off state is stable. | Highly adopted in multi-tenant SaaS: Allows selective enablement. For example, you might turn on a beta feature for Tenant A while Tenants B and C remain on the old experience, all on the same app version. This not only tailors the rollout per tenant but also lets you honor certain tenant requests (e.g., some clients may opt out of new UIs temporarily). Feature flags are a fundamental part of safe deployment practices at companies like Facebook, Amazon, etc., to ramp features globally in phases. |

*Table 1 -- **Deployment frameworks** to achieve reliable, low-downtime updates, with their characteristics and usage in multi-tenant contexts.*

In practice, these strategies can be combined (e.g., **blue-green** deployments often use **feature flags** to slowly enable features after the new version is live, adding another safety net [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/)).

Beyond application code updates, **vulnerability patching** (OS and library updates) follows similar principles. The **immutable image** approach is especially popular for security patching: instead of running apt-get update on live servers (which might require reboots), ops teams build new VM images or containers with patches and rotate them in
without downtime [\[5\]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html).
When in-place patching is unavoidable, a **rolling patch schedule** or **maintenance window** is used to patch subsets of servers at a time, so others keep the service running [\[3\]\[3\]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/).

## AWS Tools & Capabilities for Safe Patching

**Amazon Web Services (AWS)** provides an ecosystem of services to implement these strategies and automate patching/updating across multi-account setups:

- **AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager:** A service to **automate OS patching** on EC2 instances (and on-prem servers via SSM Agent). You can define **patch baselines** (which updates are approved), schedule patches using **Maintenance Windows**, and target groups of instances (by tags or resource groups) [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). Patch Manager can orchestrate **rolling patch waves**: for example, tag instances in "Patch Group A" and "B" -- patch A first, reboot, then B -- to ensure not all instances reboot at once. It also integrates with AWS Organizations for **multi-account patching**, allowing a central account to manage patches across all accounts [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). Regular, consistent patching via this service improves reliability by reducing unplanned downtime from missed vulnerabilities [\[7\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching).

- **AWS Elastic Load Balancing & Auto Scaling:** These foundational services enable many update strategies. For instance, to do a **blue-green deployment** on EC2, you might have one Auto Scaling Group (ASG) serving production (blue) and launch a second ASG with the new AMI (green). Using an Application Load Balancer, you can shift traffic to the new ASG when ready. Similarly, ASGs support **rolling updates** by replacing instances gradually (for example, AWS CloudFormation can update an ASG in batches). These ensure capacity during updates and allow quick rollback (e.g., point the load balancer back to the original ASG if issues arise).

- **AWS CodeDeploy & CodePipeline:** These DevOps services provide out-of-the-box support for **blue-green and canary deployments**. With CodeDeploy, you can deploy a new version of an application to a *replacement environment* and automatically switch traffic over via an ELB when health checks pass [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). It also supports **canary** for Lambda functions and ECS: e.g., shift 10% traffic to new version, then 90%. Crucially, CodeDeploy can be configured to **automatically rollback** if deployment steps or health tests fail [\[1\]\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). This automation is aligned with AWS best practices (the AWS Well-Architected framework advises having automated rollback triggers for deployments to minimize MTTR) [\[5\]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). CodePipeline can orchestrate the entire CI/CD flow (build -\> test -\> deploy via CodeDeploy) to make updates routine and less error-prone.

- **Amazon EKS (Kubernetes) and ECS:** For containerized apps, AWS leverages orchestrators for rolling updates. Kubernetes on EKS will do rolling updates by default (with max surge and unavailable controls), ensuring no downtime if configured right. AWS ECS now has built-in **blue-green** (e.g., through AWS App Mesh or using ECS with CodeDeploy hooks) to swap task sets behind a load balancer without loss of availability. These are vital for microservices architectures in multi-tenant systems, where dozens of services might be updating independently.

- **AWS Lambda and Serverless deployments:** Lambda versions and aliases enable a form of canary: you can publish a new version of a function and route a percentage of invokes to it (using weighted aliases). This is analogous to canary releasing a microservice. AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) or CodeDeploy can automate rolling out Lambda updates with traffic shifting. This is relevant if parts of your SaaS are serverless (ensuring even serverless updates don't break multi-tenant workloads).

- **AWS Systems Manager Automation & OpsCenter:** For multi-account scenarios, AWS provides **Automation runbooks** and EventBridge scheduling to coordinate tasks like patching across accounts [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). A blog example shows using a central **EventBridge + Lambda** to invoke patching on all accounts on a schedule [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). The runbook runs AWS-RunPatchBaseline (SSM document) on target instances in each account, using resource groups to select them [\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). The result is a **coordinated patch window** where each account's instances patch in parallel (with admin control over concurrency and error thresholds [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/)). AWS also introduced **Patch Policies** that let you set org-wide patch rules from one place [\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/).

- **AWS Kernel Live Patching:** AWS provides live patching for Linux kernels (Amazon Linux) -- allowing critical patches to apply **without reboot** [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). This niche capability helps reduce downtime for kernel updates specifically. Combined with Patch Manager for regular updates, it means even kernel vulnerabilities can be addressed with minimal service impact (the instance remains up while its kernel is patched in memory).

### Multi-Tenancy on AWS

AWS best practices for SaaS often suggest isolating tenants as much as feasible (e.g., separate accounts or separate compute clusters per major customer). Tools like Patch Manager treat each account's resources separately, so a failure patching one account doesn't affect others. Meanwhile, deployment services like CodeDeploy can target multiple ASGs or multiple ECS clusters if needed, but typically a multi-tenant provider would deploy the same update to all tenant environments (with canary on one environment first). AWS Organizations features and cross-account roles make it possible to have a **central operations team rolling out updates to all tenant accounts** in a controlled fashion [\[6\]\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). This centralized approach with proper isolation achieves consistency
while containing faults.

## Azure Tools & Capabilities for Safe Patching

**Microsoft Azure** offers analogous solutions for patching and deployment, often with a focus on integrated, PaaS-friendly approaches:

- **Azure Update Manager (Preview):** Azure's new unified tool (replacing "Update Management") to **automate patching across VMs**, with support for **cross-subscription patching** [\[7\]\[7\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching). This means if you operate a SaaS with resources in multiple Azure subscriptions, you can define one patch job to cover all. Key features include scheduling update deployments, dynamic groups of VMs (including on-prem or Azure Stack via Azure Arc), and compliance reporting. By keeping VMs **regularly patched across all subs** from a central dashboard, Azure Update Manager improves reliability and consistency [\[7\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching). You can create maintenance configurations that specify reboot options and patch categories, and scope them to many VMs. Like AWS, Azure supports the concept of patch **orchestration in waves**: you could patch, say, 20% of VMs at a time by grouping or by using Update Domains (if in an availability set). Azure also introduced **hotpatching** for Windows Server Azure Edition -- allowing certain Windows updates with no reboot -- further reducing patch downtime.

- **Azure App Service Deployment Slots:** This feature directly implements **blue-green** deployments for web apps. You get (for example) a "production" slot and a "staging" slot. You deploy the new version to staging, warm it up, then **swap slots**, which makes staging live and moves the old version to an inactive slot. The swap is orchestrated to avoid drops (it even swaps environment variables and connection strings appropriate to each slot). If something's wrong, you swap back. Slots are heavily used for multi-tenant SaaS apps on App Service because they give full **zero-downtime deployment** with one click. Azure Functions and Azure Static Web Apps have similar slot concepts. For container apps or VMs, Azure solutions like **Traffic Manager** or **Azure Front Door** can be used to achieve blue-green: deploy new instances in a new cluster or deployment, then re-route traffic at the global load balancer level.

- **Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions:** Microsoft's CI/CD platforms support pipelines with **approval gates, canary deployments, and automation**. For example, using **Azure Pipelines**, you can set up a deployment to run in stages: first to a "Canary" environment (or a subset of instances), then wait for monitoring feedback (Azure Monitor metrics or manual approval), then to full production. This can be paired with Azure Monitor alerts to automatically rollback if CPU, error rate, or other metrics degrade after an update (similar to AWS CodeDeploy rollback on alarm). Azure DevOps can also integrate with **feature flag services** (like LaunchDarkly or Azure's own Feature Management) to turn features on gradually [\[1\]\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). Many Azure-based SaaS teams use a **ring deployment model** internally -- e.g., Ring 0 (internal testers), Ring 1 (early adopters), Ring 2 (all customers) which is a form of canary release in increments.

- **Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS):** On AKS, deployments are typically done with Kubernetes rolling updates or blue-green (using separate deployments or tools like Argo Rollouts). Azure supports service mesh integrations (like Istio or Linkerd via Arc or OSS) that can do traffic splitting for canaries. Also, **Azure Container Apps** and **Service Fabric** have built-in upgrade models. **Service Fabric**, for instance, divides nodes into upgrade domains and upgrades one domain at a time (rolling), and can auto-rollback if an upgrade domain's nodes report unhealthy. It also supports blue-green-like swaps for microservices. These platform capabilities ensure that even complex stateful services (like those on Service Fabric or AKS) can be updated with minimal downtime.

- **Database Deployment support:** A big part of minimizing downtime is handling schema or database updates. Azure provides features like **SQL Database online migrations** and **Epoch-based schemas** in its guidance [\[4\]\[4\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/devops/operate/achieving-no-downtime-versioned-service-updates). While not a tool, a practice: design your database changes in a backward-compatible way (Azure's guidance is to **version your services and roll out DB changes in phases** [\[4\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/devops/operate/achieving-no-downtime-versioned-service-updates) -- e.g., deploy code that can work with both old/new schema, then apply schema change, then remove old paths). Azure's managed database services (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB) often support online indexing or live-add column operations to avoid heavy locks. Azure even allows replication and failover for some DBs so you can do a blue-green at the database level by failing over to a new updated instance. These measures align with avoiding tenant downtime during data layer changes -- often the hardest part of updates.

- **Feature Management (LaunchDarkly/Azure AppConfig):** Azure App Configuration has a feature manager that works with .NET, Java, etc., enabling easy use of **feature flags** [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). This, combined with Azure's monitoring, means you can deploy new code and leave features off until metrics are good. The official Azure SaaS framework documentation encourages using feature flags to let specific tenants opt-in to new features or to gradually release changes without impacting all tenants at once [\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#multi-tenancy-on-azure]

### Multi-Tenancy on Azure

Microsoft's guidance for SaaS emphasizes understanding tenant needs and possibly doing **tenant-by-tenant rollouts** [\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates). Unlike AWS (where accounts are common isolation), Azure multi-tenant solutions often use a single subscription with logical isolation. Thus, Azure suggests strategies like: *deploy updates to a subset of tenants first*, maybe by having those tenants on a specific **stamp** or marked for a certain slot, then expanding [\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates). The "deployment stamps" pattern (multiple identical deployments, each serving a portion of tenants) is recommended for scaling and isolation [\[3\]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/). It lends itself to safe patching: you can update one stamp at a time (rolling through stamps). For example, if you have 5 stamps (each a separate App Service instance or AKS cluster running the SaaS), do one stamp (20% of tenants) as a canary -- if all good, proceed to the others. Azure's native tooling (Update Manager, Pipeline stages, slots) can facilitate this controlled rollout. Azure also stresses **communication and transparency** with tenants around updates -- since some enterprise customers may have blackout periods, etc., it's often about finding a balance between agility and customer comfort [\[2\]\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#comparing-aws-and-azure-approaches]

## Comparing AWS and Azure Approaches

Both AWS and Azure cover the core strategies (blue-green, rolling, canary, etc.) but through different services. The table below compares how key frameworks/tools are applied in AWS vs Azure, including their reliability, downtime mitigation, rollback, and multi-tenant notes:

| **Patching/Deployment Approach** | **AWS (Tools & Services)** | **Azure (Tools & Services)** | **Reliability & Downtime Considerations** | **Rollback Mechanisms** | **Adoption in Multi-Tenant Environments** |
|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Automated OS Patching** *(Keeping VM OS updated with security patches)* | Systems Manager Patch Manager -- Define patch baselines (approved updates), target by tags or resource groups, schedule via Maintenance Windows [[6]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). Supports Linux and Windows, plus on-prem via Hybrid Runbook Workers. Can operate across multiple accounts (via Organizations integration) [[6]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/). | Azure Update Manager -- Create update deployments for VMs, with time window and reboot options. New cross-subscription support allows one job to cover many subscriptions [[7]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching). Integrates with Azure Arc to include on-prem or other clouds. | Both automate a normally error-prone task, ensuring patches are applied consistently and on schedule. They reduce the window of vulnerability (improving uptime by preventing incidents) [[7]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching). By staggering patch installation and using maintenance windows off-hours, they keep services running (e.g., patch one fault domain at a time in Azure, or one patch group at a time in AWS) so that not all VMs reboot together. Downtime is minimized to a brief reboot per VM, often unnoticed if other VM instances cover traffic. | These systems typically don't auto-rollback patches -- the assumption is testing was done prior. If a bad patch is applied, remediation might mean uninstalling that patch or restoring a VM snapshot. Thus, best practice is to patch a test environment or small subset first (which both tools allow via scoping) and use features like Azure Update Manager's dynamic groups to patch, say, a "test" tag then "prod" tag [[7]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching). In AWS, you might have patch groups "canary" and "production" and schedule them in sequence. | In multi-tenant setups with isolated VMs per tenant or per group, these tools shine: one central config can patch all VM instances across tenants. Each tenant's environment gets patched in coordination, improving overall security posture. Tenants might be unaware patching is happening if done well. If a tenant has especially sensitive uptime requirements, you might exclude their VMs to a separate schedule. Azure Update Manager's cross-subscription mode is explicitly built for organizations with many subs (common in multi-tenant solutions where each customer is in a separate sub for isolation). |
| **Application Blue-Green Deploy** *(Deploy new application version to parallel environment)* | CodeDeploy Blue/Green -- Automates creating new fleet (for EC2/ECS) and shifting traffic via ELB [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). Also supports blue-green for serverless (Lambda). Alternatively, use Auto Scaling with two groups and Route 53 weighted routing for custom blue-green. | App Service Slots -- Instantly swap staging ↔ production slots for web apps with zero downtime. For IaaS or Kubernetes, use Traffic Manager or Front Door to route between old and new deployments, or Service Fabric's swap. | Both achieve zero or near-zero downtime by pre-deploying the new version. In AWS, CodeDeploy blue/green ensures the new instances only start receiving traffic after a confirmation (and it can keep the old ones around until you confirm success). In Azure, slot swapping is designed not to drop requests, and it warms up the new instance before switching. The reliability comes from the fact that the old version is untouched and can quickly take back over if needed. | AWS: CodeDeploy can auto-revert if post-deploy health checks fail -- basically flipping back the target groups (or not switching at all if tests fail) [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). Azure: slot swap makes rollback easy -- just swap again. Even if you tear down the old slot after a successful deploy, Azure slots keep the last deployment on standby until you deploy something else, so a swap-back is possible shortly after. For more manual blue-green (VMs/containers), rollback = point traffic back to old IP/endpoint, which can usually be scripted or done in the load balancer config quickly. | Many SaaS providers use blue-green for major version upgrades. AWS users might script two parallel stacks (perhaps per tenant if tenants are isolated) -- update one while the other serves, then cutover. Azure's slots are often per app (all tenants on that app swap together), so some SaaS with very large tenants might instead use the "stamp" approach: update one stamp via slot swap (or new stamp deployment), migrate a few tenants to it, then progressively migrate others. Communication to tenants is minimal because ideally they don't see downtime, though they may notice a brief failover or increased latency during DNS switch. |
| **Gradual/Canary Deploy** *(Incremental rollout of new version)* | ALB & Route 53 Weighted Routing -- Can direct a small % of traffic to a new instance group or Lambda alias. AWS App Mesh (for microservices) can do fine-grained traffic splitting for canaries. CodeDeploy Canary -- Built-in for Lambdas (and ECS): automatically shift traffic in two increments (e.g., 10% then 90%). | Front Door / Traffic Manager -- Support weighted routing between endpoints for web traffic. Azure DevOps Release Rings -- Pipelines can implement rings (deploy to Ring 0 group, then Ring 1, etc.). Also, feature flags via App Configuration to progressively enable features to users, which is canary at the user level. | Both platforms allow serving *two versions concurrently* to real users, which is the essence of canary. This means if the new version has issues, only the canary portion suffers while the rest of users are on the stable version -- ensuring most tenants have no disruption. The key reliability aspect is monitoring: both AWS and Azure provide robust monitoring (CloudWatch, Azure Monitor) and even automated analysis (like AWS CodeGuru, etc.) to evaluate canary health. Properly used, canaries almost eliminate the risk of a full-scale bad deployment. Downtime isn't introduced; worst case, the canary portion gets errors (but those users still often have service, albeit with a glitch). | AWS can halt or rollback automatically -- e.g., CodeDeploy can stop at 10% if alarms trigger, leaving 90% users unaffected. Azure's approach often relies on manual or scripted rollback: if metrics for the new version's endpoint degrade, remove it from Front Door rotation. However, Azure's culture of "rings" often includes internal tools to automate promotion or rollback between rings. Using feature flags, a rollback means flipping the feature off globally (which essentially instantly "rolls back" user experience to the old code path, without redeploying). | In multi-tenant apps, a *tenant-based canary* is common: e.g., pick one or two customer tenants to receive the new version (perhaps by deploying their instances on a new app service slot or enabling a new feature flag for them). This way, you contain any tenant-specific issues. Both AWS and Azure support routing rules by user or tenant ID at the application level (this isn't directly a feature of ALB or Front Door, but can be implemented in the app or via edge logic). Big SaaS providers like Office 365 use this model (a few tenants get updates early, observed under real usage) [[2]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates). Once confidence is gained, the update is rolled out to all tenants. |
| **Immutable Image Patching** *(Bake updates into new VM/container images and redeploy)* | EC2 Image Builder & ECR: AWS advises building updated AMIs or container images for each patch cycle [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). These images go through test pipelines. Deployment can then use Auto Scaling rolling updates or blue-green with new images. AWS also offers AMI patching automation -- e.g., scheduled pipelines that ingest Windows/Linux updates and produce a new "Golden Image" monthly [[5]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html). | Azure Image Builder & Scale Sets: Azure Image Builder (built on HashiCorp Packer) can automate image creation with latest patches. VM Scale Sets can then do a rolling upgrade to a new image version (with health probe integration). For containers, Azure Container Registry holds new images, and AKS will pull and deploy new pods accordingly. Azure has Hotpatch for some Windows, but that's in-place -- the immutable approach in Azure would be using new VM images or containers for changes. | Immutable deployments mean the *deployment itself* handles downtime mitigation -- typically via rolling or blue-green as noted. The reliability is very high because each instance is uniform and tested. Azure's VM Scale Set rolling upgrade will automatically wait for an updated instance to be healthy before moving on, ensuring the app stays available. Likewise, AWS Auto Scaling can be configured to replace instances gradually. If using blue-green with images, see above. The main difference is that here even "patches" (OS updates) are done via replacement, removing uncertainty. | Rollback is easy: keep the previous image version. In Azure, you'd instruct the scale set to roll back to the last image (or simply stop the upgrade and redeploy VMs with the old image). In AWS, one can just re-select the old AMI for the auto scale group launch config and scale back up. Container registries keep old tags, so redeploying the previous tag is trivial. Because no in-place change happened, the old instances or containers are still there until you remove them -- so you often still have running copies of the old version until you're satisfied to shut them down. | Both clouds encourage this for multi-tenant solutions, as it yields consistency. For example, an SaaS provider might publish a new Docker image of their app and deploy it to all tenant environments gradually. If each tenant is in a separate VM or container, you update those one by one. Even if tenants share the app, using images ensures the environment is the same in all regions/for all tenants. It's common to integrate image pipelines with CI/CD so that security patches trigger a new image build and automated test, then that image is promoted. Many organizations combine this with canary: deploy the new image to a small tenant or environment first, then to all. |
| **Feature Flags (Feature Toggle)** *(Decoupling feature release from code deployment)* | AWS AppConfig (part of Systems Manager) or third-party services (LaunchDarkly, CloudBees, etc.) are used to manage feature flags. AWS AppConfig can host dynamic configs and gradually deploy configuration changes (including feature flags) in a controlled way to applications, including shutting off if anomalies detected. | Azure App Configuration provides a Feature Manager library to roll out features gradually [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). It can target user segments or % of requests. Microsoft Feature Management libraries integrate with .NET, Java, etc., to check feature flags. Also, Azure's own internal services (like Feature Flighting Service for O365) are not public, but the concept is widely adopted. | Not directly tied to downtime, but feature flags dramatically reduce risk of enabling new functionality. They provide a safety lever entirely in software. Downtime can be avoided because you don't redeploy to undo a bad feature -- you just toggle it off [[1]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/). The reliability of the overall system is improved by containing faults (e.g., one new module can be turned off without affecting everything else). Cloud providers even use this for config changes -- gradually rolling out config updates to ensure stability, which can prevent incidents | Rollback is *near-instant:* simply turn off the flag or roll back to an older configuration. For example, if a new search feature causes errors, disable the "NewSearchUI" flag and all users immediately go back to the old path. No code change, no waiting for VMs to swap -- the next request served will use old logic. This complements other rollback methods: even if a deployment succeeded technically, you might discover a business logic bug -- feature flags let you mitigate impact faster than a redeploy could. | Integral to multi-tenant SaaS operations. Often different tenants get features at different times -- feature flags allow that control. For instance, a premium tenant might get a new analytics page early. Or if one tenant reports an issue after an update, support can turn off that feature for just that tenant as a workaround. Both AWS and Azure support targeting flags by cloud context (e.g., user ID, tenant ID, geography). Feature flags are considered a must for continuous deployment environments: they enable the "test in production" approach safely and give ops more control to ensure tenant uptime. |
| **Rolling Update** *(Update servers or containers in batches, one after the other, until all are updated)* | Auto Scaling Groups with Rolling Updates -- Configure ASG to replace instances gradually with new AMI or launch template. ECS Rolling Updates -- Replace tasks one by one while maintaining service availability. EKS -- Kubernetes native rolling updates with configurable surge and unavailable settings. | VM Scale Sets Rolling Upgrade -- Automatically upgrade VMs in batches with health checks between each batch. AKS Rolling Updates -- Kubernetes orchestrated updates with configurable parameters. Service Fabric Rolling Upgrades -- Update services across upgrade domains with automatic health validation. | Changes are introduced gradually, limiting impact of any single update to a fraction of infrastructure. Service capacity is slightly reduced during updates but not completely taken down. Health checks ensure each instance is stable before proceeding to the next batch. Both platforms can achieve zero downtime if the system is designed to handle N-1 capacity during the rolling process. | If update fails on particular instances, the rolling process can pause automatically. Both platforms support automatic rollback triggers based on health check failures. Manual intervention can trigger rollback of already updated instances. Rollback isn't as instant as blue-green but typically only affects a subset of the infrastructure rather than the entire fleet. | Standard approach for large-scale infrastructure updates in multi-tenant environments. All tenants remain served as some instances always run the previous version until rollout completes. Requires backward compatibility -- new code must work with data from tenants still on old versions. Both AWS and Azure provide controls for rollout speed and error thresholds to balance update speed with stability. |

*Table 2 -- **AWS vs. Azure** tools and strategies for safe patching and
deployment.*

Both platforms achieve similar outcomes --- high availability during
updates --- but via different services. AWS leans on Systems Manager for
patching and Codedeploy/Auto Scaling for deployments; Azure leans on
Update Manager and its PaaS deployment features (slots, etc.). Each has
answers for multi-tenant scenarios (AWS with organizational tooling and
separation, Azure with emphasis on deployment design and ring
deployments).

[strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01.md#recommended-way-forward]

## Recommended Way Forward

Given these options, here's a **recommended approach** to implement
patching and updates on multi-tenant AWS/Azure infrastructure with
minimal downtime:

1. **Adopt a Multi-Tier Deployment Strategy:** Use a combination of
    **blue-green deployment** and **canary releases** for application
    updates. In practice, this means set up the ability to deploy a new
    version in parallel (new environment or slot), and initially route a
    small percentage of traffic or a subset of tenants to it
    [\[3\]](https://umatechnology.org/patch-management-in-isolated-tenant-networks-that-meet-zero-downtime-goals/).
    This provides two layers of safety: first test on the parallel
    environment, then test on a small user base in production, before
    full rollout. Both AWS and Azure support this -- e.g., AWS with
    CodeDeploy or Route 53 weighting, Azure with deployment slots or
    Traffic Manager.

2. **Implement Immutable Infrastructure for Patches:** Where possible,
    avoid in-place patching. Instead, **automate the build of new
    images** (AMI or container) with the latest patches (using AWS Image
    Builder
    [\[5\]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html)
    or Azure Image Builder) and deploy those via rolling update. This
    ensures consistency and reduces configuration drift. For example,
    for monthly OS updates, bake a patched AMI and update your Auto
    Scaling Groups gradually. In Azure, with VM Scale Sets, prepare a
    new VM image and let the scale set model upgrade VMs one by one.
    Immutable deployments reduce the risk that applying a patch will
    have unpredictable effects -- you know exactly what you're deploying
    since it's pre-tested
    [\[5\]](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2025-02-25/framework/ops_dev_integ_patch_mgmt.html).

3. **Use Automation Tools for Bulk Patching:** Leverage **AWS Systems
    Manager Patch Manager** and **Azure Update Manager** for the heavy
    lifting of OS and middleware patching across your fleet. These tools
    will help schedule patches in defined windows and ensure you cover
    all resources (including across accounts or subscriptions)
    [\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/)[\[7\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/cross-subscription-patching).
    Configure Patch Manager maintenance windows or Azure maintenance
    configurations for off-peak times, and use tags to create patch
    waves (patch a small group, then next, etc.). Turn on compliance
    reporting to track patch status. Automation here is key -- it's
    nearly impossible to manually patch dozens of VMs or container nodes
    without missing something or causing accidental downtime.

4. **Integrate Health Monitoring and Rollback Hooks:** For any
    deployment of code or image updates, have automatic health checks
    and rollback on failure. In AWS, for instance, CodeDeploy can be set
    to watch a CloudWatch alarm (like high error rate) and rollback if
    triggered
    [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/).
    In Azure, use Application Insights or Azure Monitor alerts during
    deployment slots testing; if an alert fires, abort the swap. Also
    implement **graceful shutdown and startup** scripts: when you drop a
    node out (for update or replacement), ensure it stops taking traffic
    (drain connections) before shutting down, and new nodes signal
    readiness only when the app is fully started. This avoids any
    transient errors during rotations.

5. **Gradual Tenant-by-Tenant Rollouts:** If your architecture allows,
    update a few tenants at a time instead of all at once
    [\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).
    For example, if each tenant is on a separate instance or namespace,
    update a handful, verify health (and perhaps get the tenants'
    confirmation if they are beta testers), then proceed to others. If
    using a shared environment, you can still stage rollouts by enabling
    features for one tenant at a time using feature flags. This phased
    approach ensures that if a particular tenant's data or usage pattern
    exposes a bug, you catch it early. It aligns with the **rings**
    model used by many SaaS providers (often an "early access" ring and
    a general ring).

6. **Employ Feature Flags for Risky Changes:** Incorporate a feature
    flag system especially for any update that carries significant risk
    (new features, schema changes, etc.). Deploy the code in an off
    state. Once the new version is running (say, after a blue-green
    swap), enable the feature for a small set of users or one tenant.
    Gradually increase if all is well
    [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/).
    If any issue arises that wasn't caught in testing, use the flag to
    disable the feature immediately, without rolling back the whole
    deployment
    [\[1\]](https://umatechnology.org/downtime-prevention-in-multi-tenant-hosting-under-cloud-native-workloads/).
    This strategy can save you from having to do emergency redeploys and
    can make even larger changes essentially invisible to users until
    you're confident to turn them on.

7. **Regularly Update and Test "Standby" Environments:** Keep an
    environment (or slot) updated with the latest code *even if not
    live*, as a standby. This could be a staging slot in Azure or an
    unused green environment in AWS. This environment can be used to
    test patches in production-like conditions (with production data
    samples but isolated). It also can serve as a quick fallback if
    something catastrophic happens to production -- you at least have a
    recently updated copy to switch to. Regularly rehearse the switch
    and rollback process in a non-prod environment to iron out any
    scripting issues
    [\[6\]](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/scheduling-centralized-multi-account-multi-region-patching-aws-systems-manager-automation/)
    (essentially, **fire-drills** for your deployment team).

8. **Communication & Window Planning:** While the goal is zero
    downtime, maintain a communicated **maintenance window** as a
    just-in-case and for customer awareness
    [\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).
    For instance, "We deploy updates on Wednesdays at 2AM UTC." If using
    blue-green/canary properly, users won't feel it, but if something
    goes wrong, you have that window to fix forward or rollback with
    less surprise. Be ready to use that window to do, say, a schema
    migration that might lock the DB for a few seconds, etc., but try to
    minimize impact. Communication is especially important in
    multi-tenant B2B scenarios: some customers might have policies about
    changes. As Microsoft's SaaS guidance notes, finding a balance is
    key -- you might allow customers to defer non-critical updates a few
    days, but not skip security patches
    [\[2\]\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).
    Make sure your process is transparent enough that customers trust
    updates are low-risk.

9. **Continuous Improvement:** After each patch or update, do a quick
    **post-mortem or review**. If there were any hiccups (even minor,
    like a deployment taking longer than expected or a transient error
    spike), analyze and improve the process. Over time, this will refine
    your automation scripts, health checks, and runbooks so that
    patching becomes routine. Also, keep an eye on new features from
    AWS/Azure (for example, Azure's hotpatch or AWS's new container
    deployment options) that can further reduce downtime for updates.

By following these steps, you can establish a robust patching and
deployment pipeline that keeps your multi-tenant cloud service both
**up-to-date and highly available**. In summary, **minimize in-place
changes, maximize automation, and stage everything**. Use the
cloud-native tools at your disposal: let AWS or Azure handle as much of
the heavy lifting as possible (they have invested heavily in these
capabilities). The end-state is a system where security patches are
applied consistently without breaking things, and new features/code are
rolled out like a smooth, non-event for your customers. As the Azure
Architecture Center succinctly puts it: *outage windows don't have to be
a reality for modern cloud services -- design and plan for updates that
users don't even notice*
[\[2\]](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/updates).
With the right frameworks in place, you can achieve that ideal of
transparent, continuous improvement in your cloud platform.

## Appendix A: Strategy Comparison Table

Below is a side-by-side comparison table of the five main patching and
deployment strategies, followed by a decision matrix to help select the
right approach based on specific goals and constraints:

| **Strategy** | **Downtime** | **Rollback Speed** | **Risk Mitigation** | **Infrastructure Cost** | **Complexity** | **Best Use Cases** |
|--------------|--------------|-------------------|---------------------|------------------------|----------------|-------------------|
| **Blue-Green Deployment** | Near-zero | Instant (traffic switch) | High -- full validation before go-live | High (duplicate envs) | Medium | Major version upgrades, production cutovers, high-availability SaaS |
| **Canary Release** | Minimal (localized) | Fast (halt or revert) | Very High -- gradual exposure | Medium | High | Feature rollouts, performance tuning, risk-sensitive updates |
| **Rolling Update** | Minimal | Moderate (partial revert) | Medium -- staged rollout | Low | Medium | OS patching, container updates, infrastructure refresh |
| **Immutable Infrastructure** | Zero (if orchestrated) | Easy (revert image) | High -- consistent, tested builds | Medium | High | Security patching, compliance-driven updates, large-scale fleet management |
| **Feature Flags** | None | Instant (toggle off) | Very High -- decouples release & deploy | Low | High (in-code logic) | Gradual feature exposure, tenant-specific features, A/B testing |

## Appendix B: Decision Matrix

Use this matrix to help determine which strategy (or combination) is
most appropriate based on the scenario:

| **Decision Criteria** | **Recommended Strategy** |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Need to update with zero downtime | Blue-Green, Immutable Infrastructure, Feature Flags |
| Want to test updates on a small subset first | Canary Release, Feature Flags |
| Need fast rollback in case of failure | Blue-Green, Feature Flags |
| Updating OS or base infrastructure | Rolling Update, Immutable Infrastructure |
| Updating application code | Blue-Green, Canary Release, Feature Flags |
| Multi-tenant environment with shared resources | Feature Flags, Canary Release (with tenant targeting), Immutable Infrastructure |
| Limited infrastructure budget | Rolling Update, Feature Flags |
| High compliance or audit requirements | Immutable Infrastructure, Blue-Green (with version tracking) |
| Frequent small updates | Rolling Update, Feature Flags |
| Complex or risky new features | Canary Release + Feature Flags |
